sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses the abuse of children in foster care, restraint, the drugging of children, and the deaths of children. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Foster care is not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track foster homes, foster care agencies or state child welfare systems. We do track the therapeutic group homes and residential treatment centers where states place children from foster care; they are in our [directory](/tti-program-index/).

When a state takes a child into its custody, it can send that child to the same residential treatment centers parents pay for. Many have no demonstrated treatment needs, some are sent to other states, and the companies that hold them are paid by the day. Children in their care have been restrained to death, drugged and sexually abused, and no one can count how often it happens.

We are not experts on foster care. The people who grew up in it, and the organizations listed below, are.

sections.label: The state decides where a child lives
sections.heading: The state decides where a child lives
sections.body:
A child in foster care is in the custody of a state, county or tribal agency, placed there by a court. The agency, not a parent, decides where the child lives.

The power to take poor children and place them is old. In *Ex parte Crouse* (1838) the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the state's right to confine a child without due process ([disability timeline](/idd-timeline/)). From 1854 to 1929 the orphan trains sent children west to families who often used them as labor, and many were not orphans: in one charity's figures for 1857 to 1858, 65 percent had at least one living parent ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)).[^1] Foster care began to replace orphanages after the 1909 White House Conference on Dependent Children. When the orphanages emptied between the 1960s and 1980s, poor children moved into psychiatric and behavioral facilities ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)), and residential treatment has been one of the places a state sends children ever since.

Most children in foster care today live with relatives or in foster homes. A shrinking but still large number live in institutions.

Table: Children in foster care
| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| In foster care on September 30, 2024 | 328,947[^2] |
| Spent time in foster care during fiscal year 2024 | 505,682[^2] |
| Living with relatives, 2024 | 39 percent[^2] |
| In non-relative foster homes, 2024 | 28 percent[^2] |
| In therapeutic foster homes, 2024 | 28,365[^2] |
| In group homes, institutions or residential care, 2024 | About 35,000[^2] |
| Last placed in a residential facility, 2002 | About 101,000 (19 percent)[^3] |
| Last placed in a residential facility, 2022 | About 34,000 (9 percent)[^3] |

States keep custody but hand most of the work to private agencies. In a 2015 Senate Finance Committee survey, 31 of the 33 states that answered used private agencies, and 16 contracted with for-profit providers as well as nonprofits.[^4] Private agencies recruit and supervise foster homes and run therapeutic foster care, group homes, shelters and residential treatment. Medicaid pays residential treatment a daily rate for each child.[^5]

sections.label: Sent to the same facilities
sections.heading: Sent to the same facilities
sections.body:
The residential treatment centers that take children from foster care are the ones parents pay for. The Senate Finance Committee's 2024 investigation of Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health and Vivant Behavioral Healthcare found that "a significant portion of foster children placed at RTFs have no demonstrated behavioral health needs." In 2013, 28.8 percent of children in congregate care had "No Clinical Indicators."[^5] ([Our summary of the report](/warehouses-of-neglect/).) All four companies are in our records: [Universal Health Services](/operator/universal-health-services/) with more than 70 programs, [Devereux](/operator/devereux-advanced-behavioral-health/) with 43, [Acadia Healthcare](/operator/acadia-healthcare/) with 13 and [Vivant Behavioral Health](/operator/vivant-behavioral-health/) with 5.

Sequel Youth & Family Services shows how the business works. Jay Ripley co-founded it in 1999, after co-founding the juvenile justice contractor Youth Services International, later owned and run by James F. Slattery ([juvenile justice timeline](/juvenile-justice-timeline/)). In 2015 Ripley told an interviewer that Sequel sought children whose placements the government pays for, and that "you can make money in this business if you control staffing."[^5] Sequel passed from one private equity owner to the next from 2010 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)) and took in children from more than 40 states and territories.[^6] [Our records list 42 Sequel programs](/operator/sequel-tsi/), most now closed. In 2021 Ripley founded Vivant, which bought 13 of Sequel's facilities; three senior Vivant leaders came from Sequel, among them its former vice president of operations, who joined a month after leaving.[^5]

Some companies run foster care and youth residential programs side by side.

Table: Companies that run both
| Company | Foster care | Youth programs |
|---|---|---|
| Devereux | Recruits foster parents[^7] | 43 in our records |
| KidsPeace | Runs foster care[^8] | Campuses in Pennsylvania, Georgia and Maine and a psychiatric hospital in Pennsylvania;[^8] 4 in our records |
| Boys Town | Runs foster care[^9] | Residential programs, several in our records; began as an orphanage in 1917 |
| Youth Villages | Runs foster care[^10] | Five residential campuses in Tennessee and Georgia,[^11] in our records |
| Sevita (The MENTOR Network) | Runs foster care[^12] | NeuroRestorative's 14 group homes for young people in Illinois, in our records; owned by private equity firms since 2001 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)) |

sections.label: Sent out of state
sections.heading: Sent out of state
sections.body:
In fiscal year 2021 nearly 2,400 children in foster care were placed in residential facilities in another state.[^13] The interstate compact that governs foster placements across state lines does not cover residential treatment centers or group homes. States say they send children away because there are too few placements at home, and the children who stay wait: Kentucky's ombudsman reviewed 49 children who slept in state office buildings between June and October 2024. One stayed 35 days, and the youngest was a year old.[^14]

Far from the agency that placed them, children are harder to protect. Illinois sent foster children to Acadia-run facilities in Arkansas, Indiana and Michigan where police logs recorded assaults and reports of sexual abuse.[^15] Oregon brought every one of its out-of-state foster children home in June 2020 and ended its contract with Sequel, which held most of them.[^16]

sections.label: What happens to them
sections.heading: What happens to them
sections.body:
In 2020 staff at Lakeside Academy, a Sequel facility in Michigan, restrained Cornelius Fredericks, 16, a child in foster care, on the floor for about 12 minutes. He died, and the medical examiner ruled his death a homicide.[^17] Reporters compiled more than 8,600 emergency calls from Sequel facilities in 18 states, and found 20 cases since 2010 in which government investigators found staff in sexual or romantic relationships with residents.[^6] At Universal Health Services' Provo Canyon School in Utah, a 14-year-old Oregon foster child with an intellectual disability was physically restrained and chemically sedated more than 30 times in four months.[^5] After the Philadelphia Inquirer reported a 25-year pattern of sexual abuse by staff at Devereux, Philadelphia's child welfare and behavioral health agencies moved to remove 53 children from its facilities in 2020.[^18]

The Senate Finance Committee concluded that providers fill facilities to capacity while cutting staff to widen their margin on each day's rate, and that the abuse by staff and overuse of restraint and seclusion that follow are "endemic to the RTF operating model."[^5] The newest kind of group setting is no safer on paper. The Family First Prevention Services Act of 2018 stops federal foster care payments for a child in a group setting after 14 days unless it meets set requirements, as a Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP) does,[^13] but QRTPs are not bound by the restraint and seclusion rules that psychiatric residential treatment facilities must follow.[^5]

Children in foster care are also drugged more. The GAO found in 2011 that foster children in five states were prescribed psychotropic drugs at higher rates than other children on Medicaid; hundreds took five or more at once, and some were infants.[^19] In 2018, one in three foster children on these drugs in five states did not get the treatment planning or monitoring their states required.[^20]

Private foster care has its own record. The Senate Finance Committee's 2017 study of The MENTOR Network, then majority owned by the private equity firm Vestar Capital Partners and serving 10,300 foster children in 18 states, found that Maryland cited violations in 20 of 22 quarterly reviews and MENTOR kept operating there, and that most children who died in its care were never the subject of an internal investigation.[^4]

The young people themselves say the placements did not help. In *Away From Home*, 78 who had lived in group homes, shelters and residential treatment while in foster care described them, and most "found little to no long term value from them."[^21]

sections.label: No one counts it
sections.heading: No one counts it
sections.body: States place children in these facilities without the information to see what happens there. In 2024 the HHS Inspector General found that 16 states lacked the information to spot patterns of maltreatment in residential facilities, and 32 did not formally track whether a facility's owner ran facilities in other states. 13 did not consistently report whether a maltreated child lived in a residential facility, so the Inspector General could not count abuse in these facilities nationwide.[^13] The GAO had asked HHS in 2022 to help states share what works in preventing maltreatment in residential facilities. HHS agreed, and by June 2024 had not acted.[^3]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If a child is in danger right now**, call [911](tel:911).
- **State child protective services (CPS):** every state takes reports of child abuse and neglect, including abuse in foster homes, group homes and residential facilities. Find yours in the federal [list of state reporting numbers](https://www.childwelfare.gov/state-child-abuse-and-neglect-reporting-numbers/). Abuse in a facility is investigated by the state where the facility is, so report a child placed out of state there, and tell the child's caseworker and the agency that placed the child.
- **Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline**, call or text, 24 hours, in more than 170 languages: 1-800-422-4453. Childhelp does not take reports itself; its counselors help you reach the right agency.
- **Protection and Advocacy agencies:** every state has a federally mandated legal advocacy agency for people with disabilities, including children harmed in residential treatment centers and hospitals. [Find your state's agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

Our [reporting directory](/report-abuse/) lists each state's agencies, hotlines and licensing offices.

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [FosterClub](https://www.fosterclub.com/): A national network for young people in and from foster care, "built for youth, powered by youth," whose Lived Experience Leaders speak to lawmakers and agencies.
- [Foster Youth in Action](https://www.fosteryouthaction.org/): Founded in 2008 by foster youth organizers. A national network of youth-led groups working to change the foster care system.
- [Think of Us](https://www.thinkofus.org/): A foster care research and policy organization led and guided by people with lived experience. Publisher of *Away From Home*, on institutional placements.
- [Children's Rights](https://www.childrensrights.org/): Brings legal action against state systems, including to stop the unnecessary institutionalization of children.
- [National Center for Youth Law](https://youthlaw.org/): Impact litigation and policy work on foster care, youth justice, health and education.
- [Juvenile Law Center](https://jlc.org/): Advocates for the rights of young people in the child welfare and justice systems.
- [The Imprint](https://imprintnews.org/): An independent nonprofit daily newsroom covering child welfare and youth justice, including its "Medicated in Foster Care" series.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you grew up in foster care, work in it, or know something on this page is wrong or out of date, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.

sections.label: Date the figures were checked
sections.body: Figures checked against their sources on October 8, 2026.
